title: Vessantara gives
hook: the generous prince gives away the kingdom's rain-bringing white elephant and is exiled

segments.voice: Yesterday: ruru, the golden deer who saved the man who sold him out, and then saved him again. Your line: do it anyway.

A bag of old clothes left at the donation bin is an easy gift: things nobody wanted anyway. The good jacket is harder. A free Saturday. The last of something. Today's story lives in that harder place. It's the last of the five hundred and forty-seven Jatakas in the Pali collection, and the longest. In parts of Southeast Asia it is recited aloud at temple festivals, sometimes all in one day. It's about a prince who gives away the thing nobody wanted him to give.
screen: `THE BAG OF OLD CLOTHES.` → `THE THING YOU'D RATHER KEEP.` → `THE LAST AND LONGEST JATAKA.`

segments.voice: Vessantara is the crown prince of the Sivi kingdom, and from childhood he loves to give. The story says he wanted to give even his own heart or eyes if someone asked. His kingdom owns a treasure: a magnificent white elephant, and wherever it goes, the rain comes. Then envoys arrive from a neighboring land, Kalinga, where the rains have failed and the fields are cracking. They ask for the elephant. Vessantara, sitting on its back, pours water over their hands, the old sign of a gift, and gives it to them. Picture the city the next morning. Their rain has just walked out of the gate. The people are furious and demand his exile, and his father, the king, gives in. So Vessantara leaves the palace for a mountain in the forest, and his wife Maddi and their two small children choose to go with him. On the way out he gives away even more: his chariot, his horses. They walk the last part on foot, he and Maddi each carrying a child. Why does this story come last? Tradition says Vessantara is the Buddha's last human life before the one in which he awakens, and that here he completes the perfection of giving, dana. It isn't told as a sensible budget. It's giving taken as far as it can go. And the story doesn't hide the cost: a whole city angry, a family without a home. Tomorrow, the cost gets harder still.
screen: `THE ELEPHANT THAT BRINGS THE RAIN.` · `GIVEN TO A LAND IN DROUGHT.` · `THE CITY DEMANDS HIS EXILE.` · `THE PERFECTION OF GIVING.` · then, large: `GENEROSITY COSTS.`

segments.voice: Hold in mind one thing you have that you'd rather keep, an object, an hour, some attention, and notice where the reluctance sits: the chest, the hands, the jaw. You don't have to give it away; just breathe with the pull between keeping and giving, and let both be there. Then picture the moment of handing it over, water poured over open hands, and see what happens in the body.
Vessantara gives. The prince who gave the rain-bringing elephant, and was sent into exile for it.
Your line: generosity costs. The rain walked out of the gate, and he let it go. Day ninety-two, complete.

howItsDone: In Thailand, Laos and Cambodia the Vessantara story is recited in full at a yearly temple festival, often in a single day, and it is taught as the great story of dana, generosity.

fork.setup: you're the prince. envoys from a land in drought ask for your kingdom's rain-bringing elephant. what do you do?
options: refuse: your own people need the rain.
fork.reveal: he pours water over their hands and gives it. it costs him the palace: the city demands his exile.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: giving, generosity; Vessantara is said to complete the perfection of dana.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prince who was bad with money.
what it means: the perfection of giving, taken as far as it can go, with the cost told plainly.
what a scholar hears: Jataka 547 is the last of the ten long 'great births'; it's recited at the Thai Thet Mahachat festival and painted on temple walls across Southeast Asia.
